claims.text: Elevated temperature accelerates oxidation kinetics on Q235 steel.
Elevated-temperature exposure causes rapid formation of magnetite (Fe3O4) on Q235 steel.
The magnetite film formed at elevated temperature is dense, coherent, and adherent.
A dense magnetite film acts as a barrier to oxygen and aggressive species.
The magnetite barrier suppresses subsequent corrosion of Q235 steel in harsh environments.
At room temperature, slower oxidation kinetics produce a discontinuous or less-protective oxide film.
The room-temperature oxide film permits continued corrosion attack.
After the same exposure duration, Q235 samples exposed at elevated temperature will have a lower corrosion rate than samples exposed at room temperature.
Elevated-temperature samples will show less mass loss than room-temperature samples.
Elevated-temperature samples will have thinner and more protective oxide films than room-temperature samples.
The proposed comparison uses identically polished, previously untreated Q235 steel specimens.
Temperature is isolated by holding chloride concentration, pH, humidity, surface finish, corrosive medium, and exposure duration constant.
The elevated-temperature test condition is approximately 80°C.
The proposed protective behavior requires conditions that permit stable oxide formation and do not mechanically disrupt the film.
Extreme environments that cause oxide-film spallation may not exhibit the proposed corrosion suppression.
Failure of elevated-temperature specimens to exhibit both a denser, more coherent Fe3O4 layer and a lower corrosion rate relative to room-temperature specimens would falsify the hypothesis.
